title: Look Where I Look
description: Misdirection steers attention, not just eyes; lead their gaze with your own
tryIt: Practice The Rejected Card five times alone with a deck, then perform it for one person and notice where their eyes go when you turn the double.

concepts.title: How it works: attention is a spotlight
concepts.contentHtml:
The word misdirection sounds as if you must make people look the wrong way, but researchers define it more exactly. Macknik, Martinez-Conde and a team that included the magicians Teller, James Randi and Apollo Robbins describe misdirection as drawing the audience's attention away from the method and towards the effect.1 The method is the secret behind the trick; the effect is what the spectator perceives. The key word is attention, which behaves like a spotlight that can sit somewhere other than where the eyes point. Your job is to steer the spotlight.

The idea has a long pedigree in the trade. In 1958 the Spanish magician Arturo de Ascanio published Conception of the Magical Atmosphere, with misdirection as one of its cornerstones. He defined it as drawing the eye and attention of the public to a safe and interesting point while a secret action happens elsewhere, then called that definition poor, since misdirection could have three different grades, or levels of intensity.2 In dissolution there are two points of interest, so attention is split. In attraction the innocent point is more interesting than the secret one. In deviation the spectator's gaze and attention are both carried away.

Researchers add a second split. In overt misdirection you redirect the spectator's gaze. In covert misdirection the gaze stays put but the spotlight of attention moves, so spectators can look straight at the method and still be unaware of it. Magicians tend to prize the covert kind as more elegant, and it is the kind you will practice first, because it costs nothing: no props, no bangs, just where you look and what you ask.

concepts.title: The method: The Rejected Card
concepts.contentHtml:
The effect: you read the spectator, show them a wrong card, put it away, and the wrong card turns out to be theirs. You need your jog control and your double lift from earlier skills. The only new thing is the order of your eyes. The example cards are the 4♦ (theirs) and the K♣ (the second card).

  1. Choice. Spread the deck face down. The spectator takes any card, looks at it and remembers it. Say: "Don't tell me. Just picture it."
  2. Control. They push it back in. Chat while you use your jog control, and finish with their card on top of the deck.
  3. Eyes first. Square the deck face down in your left hand. Look them in the eye and say: "I'm going to read you, not the cards." Hold their gaze.
  4. Turn the double. Still looking at their eyes, turn the top two cards over as one and lay them face up on the deck. Only now drop your eyes to the face-up card, as if checking it. Theirs will follow. The face-up K♣ is the second card, not theirs.
  5. Reject. "That is not it, is it?" They agree. Look up again, turn the two cards back over as one and square them.
  6. Set aside. "I'll put the wrong one over here." Deal the top card (really their 4♦) face down onto the table.
  7. Reveal. Ask them to name their card out loud. Turn the tabled card over: "You rejected it yourself."

What they see is a performer studying their face, a wrong card, and a rejection. What you do is one double turnover, timed to a moment when their eyes are on yours. Common mistakes: watching your own hands during the turn, which sends their eyes to the move; dropping your eyes first and turning after; and holding the face-up card too long, which invites a closer look. Make the whole turn last about as long as a breath.

concepts.title: Myth check: they missed it because they looked away
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A spectator misses a secret move because their eyes were pointing somewhere else.
Reality Eye-tracking studies suggest that where the eyes point is not the whole story.

Kuhn and Tatler recorded the eye movements of observers as a magician made a cigarette disappear by dropping it below the table. Whether observers detected the drop could not be explained by blinks, eye movements or how far the cigarette was from the center of vision. The authors concluded that the magician primarily manipulates the spectators' attention rather than their gaze,1 using principles similar to those in inattentional-blindness studies.

Wait, really? Kuhn and Land studied the vanishing ball illusion, in which a magician only pretends to throw a ball that is hidden in the hand, and most spectators perceive it rising and vanishing in mid-air. The magician's own head and eyes follow an imaginary ball upwards, and that social cue turned out to be critical. Yet observers did not direct their gaze to the area in which they claimed to have seen the ball vanish.2 Their eyes were not fooled; their attention was.

For you, this changes the practice. Rehearsing a move until it is invisible is not enough, because the audience is not looking for it with their eyes alone. Rehearse your own eyes. Decide where you look at each beat of the trick, and let the spectator's attention follow your face, your voice and your questions. The cheapest misdirection you own is the direction of your own gaze.

title: The Off-Beat
description: Attention rises and falls; time a small move for the dip after a laugh
tryIt: Practice The Joke First until the glimpse feels like tidying up, then perform it for one person and wait for their laugh before you move.

concepts.title: How it works: attention rises and falls
concepts.contentHtml:
A good performance is a series of beats: a question, a gag, a reveal. Audience attention does not stay level through them. It climbs towards each punchline and relaxes once it has passed. In 1978 the magician Joe Bruno published Anatomy of Misdirection, which sorts techniques into distraction, diversion and relaxation. Bruno's third general principle is relaxation, which relates to the temporal fluctuations in attention created through off-beat moments in a routine.

Kuhn and colleagues, summarizing the performers' lore, say the magician may create an off-beat moment through a momentary relaxation, such as after a joke or a magical effect.1 They add that these moments are thought to reduce attention, which allows the method to be executed without being noticed. The phrase is "thought to": this is craft knowledge that experiments have only begun to test. Attentional de-emphasis can also occur once a trick has concluded, so the audience does not suspect a method at that moment. Anticipation and repetition work the same way: spectators relax when they think they know what is coming, and an action repeated several times draws less attention each time.

Humor is the classic off-beat tool. Macknik's team, which included working magicians, reports their intuition that when the audience is laughing it is as if time stops and the attentional spotlight is put on hold.2 Read that as expert intuition rather than a measurement. Still, it gives you a plan: build a small laugh into the trick, and keep your secret move for the moment just after it.

concepts.title: The method: The Joke First
concepts.contentHtml:
The effect is a deliberate flop followed by a real find. The flop is the off-beat; the glimpse of your key card hides inside it. You need Cut It Anywhere from The Key Card, and nothing else.

  1. Challenge. Hold the deck face down. Say: "Name any card, and I will find it. Badly." They name one, for instance the queen of hearts.
  2. The miss. Turn the top card face up and drop it on the table: "Close." It will not be their card (if it ever is, take the applause). Smile at the card yourself.
  3. Wait. Say nothing and do nothing. Let them laugh. This is the beat you are borrowing.
  4. Glimpse. As the laugh fades, pick up the deck, tap its edges level and tip the inner end up for a second to read the bottom card. Say it is the 7♣. Keep looking at the table card, not at the deck.
  5. Reset. "Right. Properly this time." Spread the deck face down and run Cut It Anywhere from its second step: they take a card, you split the deck, they place it, you drop the bottom half on top, they cut, you deal.

What they see is a joke that failed. What you do is square the deck, which every performer does. The timing matters: move after the punchline, not on it. At the punchline eyes are on your face; a beat later they are on the miss, and you are tidying. Common mistakes: glimpsing before the laugh while the room is quiet, rushing it so the laugh is still building, and looking down at the deck, which invites everyone else to look too. If they do not laugh, wait one more breath and make your own small joke about the miss.

concepts.title: Myth check: you need a big distraction
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A secret move needs a big distraction, such as a bang or a stunt.
Reality Performers usually prefer a quiet beat, such as the dip after a laugh.

Bruno did describe crude external distractions. A loud bang is extremely effective but can easily disrupt the performance, and so diminish the effect, so magicians usually opt instead for subtler forms, such as a well-timed cough. A relaxing beat costs the performance nothing: the audience feels a pause, not a trick.

Wait, really? Performers disagree about exactly when to move. Teller, in a 2012 Smithsonian Magazine article, wrote that a viewer has only so much attention to give, and if he is laughing, his mind is too busy with the joke to backtrack rationally, and that they often follow a secret move immediately with a joke. That is the opposite order from The Joke First: the move comes first and the laugh covers it afterwards. Kuhn and colleagues, citing Tamariz, describe the off-beat as arriving after a joke. Both are craft rules that work for their users.

Try both orders with a friend and see which feels more natural for your own patter. The principle underneath is the same: do not put the move at the peak of attention, and give it a reason to look like nothing. Teller's own rule of thumb is simple: it is hard to think critically if you are laughing.

title: Big Motion, Small Motion
description: Why we miss gorillas and swapped strangers, and how a big action covers a small one
tryIt: Practice Prediction by Reach until the peek lasts about a second, then perform it for one person with the pen and paper on the far side of the table.

concepts.title: How it works: we see less than we think
concepts.contentHtml:
In the famous gorilla study by Simons and Chabris, observers were asked to count how many times the members of a basketball team passed a ball to one another, while ignoring a different team. While they concentrated on the counting task, most observers failed to notice a person wearing a gorilla suit walk across the scene.1 This is inattentional blindness: people fail to notice an unexpected object that is fully visible. It differs from change blindness, where people fail to notice that something is different from the way it was before.

The gorilla study is not just about distraction by a second task. Memmert recorded observers' eyes and showed that many did not notice the gorilla even when they were looking directly at it.2 The lesson for a magician is the same as in the last two lessons: attention, not gaze, decides what reaches awareness, and a small secret action sitting in plain sight is routinely missed.

Performers have long exploited this with one blunt rule. Bruno identified five types of diversion, as Kuhn and colleagues summarize them. The third is disguise, where an action appears to be performed for one purpose when in reality it is done for another. Related to this is the idea that large motions will disguise small ones.3 A big, purposeful movement, such as reaching across a table, draws attention; a tiny movement elsewhere, made at that moment, stays in the shadows.

concepts.title: The method: Prediction by Reach
concepts.contentHtml:
The effect: you write a prediction, they cut the deck as freely as it seems, and the card they land on is your prediction. You need the cross-cut force from Lifts and Forces, plus one new, tiny skill, a peek at the top card. Practice the peek alone first: tip the deck towards you, lift the inner corner of the top card with your left thumb just far enough to read its index, and let it spring back. It takes a second. The example card is the 7♥.

  1. Set the scene. Hold the deck face down in your left hand, near the table edge. Put the pen and a slip of paper on the far side of the table. Say: "I need to write something down."
  2. The reach. Your right hand sweeps across the table for the pen and paper, a wide, purposeful movement. Halfway through it, your left hand peeks at the top card. Be done before your right hand arrives.
  3. Write. Write "7♥" on the slip, fold it and put it in front of the spectator.
  4. Cut. Put the deck down. They cut off about half and place it on the table. Call it A; the 7♥ is on top of A.
  5. Cross. Place the lower half across A and chat for a moment about how free the choice was.
  6. Lift. Lift off the top pile: "You cut here." Turn over the top card of A, the 7♥, then let them open the slip.

What they see is a performer going to fetch a pen. What you do is a peek, hidden inside that reach. Common mistakes: peeking when your right hand is still, so nothing is moving to cover it; stopping to look at the card; and reaching so slowly that the reach itself becomes the focus. Make the reach look as ordinary as a real reach. The pen is real, and so is your need for it.

concepts.title: Myth check: you would notice if a stranger swapped
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth You would obviously notice if the person you were talking to were swapped for someone else.
Reality In a real-world experiment about half of the pedestrians did not.

In 1998 Simons and Levin had an experimenter ask a pedestrian on a campus for directions. After 10 to 15 seconds, two other experimenters carrying a door rudely passed between them, and during the interruption the first experimenter was replaced by a different one. Despite clear differences in clothing, appearance and voice, only 7 of the 15 pedestrians reported noticing the change of experimenters.1 Those who did not notice continued the conversation as if nothing had happened.

Wait, really? In the second experiment the same two experimenters dressed as construction workers. All the younger pedestrians in the first experiment had noticed the switch, but only 4 of the 12 pedestrians in this experiment reported noticing it.2 Simons and Levin suggested that social group matters: we tend to encode the individual features of people like us, and the group features of people who are not.

The door is a large motion in itself, a big visual event that briefly occupies the scene. You can borrow the idea at a card table: when something obvious and interesting is going on, nobody tracks the small stuff. But the study should also keep you honest. People feel certain that they would notice, which is exactly why a well-covered move feels like magic and not like a blur.

title: While You Write
description: Time misdirection: do the secret work early, while their attention is on something else
tryIt: Practice While You Write until you can fan, find the key and cut in the time it takes to write a card name, then perform it for one person with a real pen and slip.

concepts.title: How it works: time misdirection
concepts.contentHtml:
So far you have hidden moves in space, with your eyes, and in the beat of a laugh. The third tool is time. Magicians deliberately separate the moment of the method from the moment of the effect, so that by the time something amazing happens the audience cannot trace it back to anything you did. The performers' name for this is time misdirection, and Kuhn and colleagues credit Leech with calling it that.1

The psychology is memory. People remember more of an event immediately after it has occurred, as compared to some time later.2 A delay therefore works as a kind of memory misdirection: the longer the gap, the less the spectator can reconstruct what happened. Macknik and colleagues describe it as a delay between method (the cause) and effect that prevents the spectator from causally linking the two. A prediction that relies on a force is an example, because the spectator forgets which card they actually cut to.

Delay alone is not enough. What the spectator does during the gap matters, and the best gap is one in which they are busy with something unconnected with your hands. Writing is ideal. A person bent over a slip of paper, concentrating on spelling out a card name, is giving you a dead time of several seconds that they believe is theirs, not yours. Kuhn and colleagues are frank that much is still unknown about which factors influence this forgetting, so treat the technique as a rule of thumb to test with real people.

concepts.title: The method: While You Write
concepts.contentHtml:
The effect: they choose a card, lose it with cuts, write its name on a slip, and you produce it as the top card of the deck. The secret is a cut that happens while their head is down. Use the key-card tools from lesson one. The example cards are the 9♣ (key) and the Q♥ (chosen).

  1. Glimpse. Square the deck and read the bottom card, the 9♣, as you chat.
  2. Choice. They take any card from a face-down spread, look at it and remember it.
  3. Place. Lift off the top half and put it on the table. They put their card on it and you drop the bottom half on top, so the 9♣ lies directly on their Q♥.
  4. Cut. Ask them to cut and complete the cut as often as they like. The ring is unbroken.
  5. The writing. Hand them a pen and a slip: "Write down the name of your card, fold it and hold it in your fist." While their head is down, pick up the deck, fan it towards yourself, low, and find the 9♣. The Q♥ is the card right after it. Cut the deck so that every card down to and including the 9♣ goes to the bottom. The Q♥ is now on top.
  6. Stop. The moment the pen stops, square the deck and put it down.
  7. Reveal. After a pause and a little talk, ask them to read the slip aloud. Turn over the top card.

What they see is a person writing and a performer doing nothing visible. What you do is a cut, hidden in time, while their attention is on their own hand. Common mistakes: fanning when they are looking at you, going on after the pen stops, and revealing at once. Leave a short pause: the delay is part of the secret. If they finish early, square up and wait.

concepts.title: Myth check: a pause kills the trick
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A pause between the secret work and the finish weakens the trick; reveal as soon as you can.
Reality The delay is one of the strongest tools you have.

Beginners rush to the reveal because the secret work makes them nervous. But the delay is what protects them. Magicians typically try to separate the method from the effect in time, and in your routine the secret work is finished before the reveal even begins. Add a pause, a question, a second small effect: all of it adds distance between what you did and what they saw.

Wait, really? The extent of forgetting also depends on what the spectator is doing during the delay, and much is still unknown about what factors influence this.1 In other words, nobody has yet measured the ideal delay, or the best filler. Performers rely on experience, and so will you: watch your spectators and notice when they look puzzled or relaxed.

Use the gap well. Fill it with something that does not point back at the secret work: a story, a question about their card, a small joke. What you say should never describe what you have just done, and it should never hurry towards the reveal.

title: Natural Action, Whole Set
description: Teller's principles, natural action, and putting three beats together into one set
tryIt: Perform The Three-Beat Set for one person from joke to reveal, with a reason for every move, and tell a friend afterwards which beat they liked best.

concepts.title: How it works: what performers and scientists share
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2012 Teller, of Penn and Teller, wrote an article for Smithsonian Magazine listing seven principles magicians use to alter your perceptions. Several you have already met: it is hard to think critically if you are laughing (lesson two), and the secret should be kept outside the frame of the trick (lesson four). Another is that to fool the mind, combine at least two tricks, because one effect can distract from the secret behind the other. This lesson uses that idea to combine all your techniques into one set.

A final principle holds everything together: natural action. Kuhn and colleagues note that magicians often talk about the need for actions to appear natural, as anything unnatural will generally arouse suspicion.1 In their example, the French Drop fails if the false transfer looks odd. Misdirection of your hands alone is not enough: every move needs a reason that fits the story, such as squaring the deck, fetching a pen or tidying up after a gag.

The science of misdirection has grown around this craft. Kuhn and colleagues propose a psychologically based taxonomy with three basic categories, corresponding to the types of psychological mechanisms affected: perception, memory and reasoning.2 Your techniques fit the headings. Gaze leading and big motions work on perception and attention. The delay of While You Write works on memory. Natural action works on reasoning, because it stops spectators suspecting a method at all.

concepts.title: The method: The Three-Beat Set
concepts.contentHtml:
The effect: a failed joke, a lost card, a written slip, and a rejected wrong card that is theirs. Each beat hides one move, and each move has a different cover. Practice the beats one at a time, then link them.

  1. Beat 1, the joke. Run The Joke First: they name a card, you turn a wrong top card, wait for the laugh, then square the deck and glimpse the bottom card as it fades.
  2. Beat 2, the choice. Run While You Write: they take a card, you place it under the key, they cut, and while they write the name on the slip you fan, find the key and cut so their card is on top.
  3. Beat 3, the reveal. Look them in the eye and ask them to picture the card. Turn the double face up while holding their gaze, then drop your eyes with theirs. "Not that, is it?" Turn the double back and deal the top card face down to the table as the wrong one.
  4. Finish. They read the slip aloud. Turn over the tabled card, their own.

The script matters as much as the moves. Write down a reason for each secret action in one short line: "tidying", "writing", "reading you". If you cannot say the reason, the move will look strange and the spectator will wonder about it. Run the whole set aloud, alone, at an even pace, and time each beat. Common mistakes: giving each beat a long wind-up, drawing a laugh you cannot control, and rushing the third beat because you are relieved the secret work is done.

concepts.title: Myth check: brain science has solved magic
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Scientists now fully understand how magicians fool us, and brain scanners will soon make magic obsolete.
Reality Magicians and scientists are still working out the details together.

Teller was skeptical. He wrote that magic is not really about the mechanics of your senses; it is about understanding, and then manipulating, how viewers digest sensory information. In the same article he wrote: "Neuroscientists are novices at deception. Magicians have done controlled testing in human perception for thousands of years." Kuhn and colleagues note that magicians are undoubtedly masters of deception, but tend to be skeptical about whether science can teach them anything about misdirection. They also say that much remains unknown, such as which factors influence how much a spectator forgets during a delay.

Wait, really? Teller recalls an experiment at the age of 11, with Cub Scouts as his test subjects. His hypothesis was that nobody would see him sneak a fishbowl under a shawl; it proved false, and the Scouts pelted him with hard candy. It is a fair summary of the field: performers have been running experiments with live audiences for centuries, and scientists are now measuring some of what the performers learned.

It is also a reminder of what all of this is. Macknik and colleagues point out that using completely natural means, magicians create effects that seem to be outside the laws of nature.1 Nobody in this course is reading minds. You are using attention, memory and timing, with a deck of cards, to make a friend smile. Misdirection is a performer's craft, and a friendly one.
